strengths: The core static idea is simple and elegant: grouping keys by a logarithmic function of predicted weight and using random tie-breaking yields an entropy-style expected depth bound for arbitrary frequency distributions. This is a clean generalization of the Zipfian-only learning-augmented treap setting discussed in the paper.
The static robustness analysis is natural and persuasive: using predicted frequencies turns the access bound into cross-entropy, giving an interpretable additive dependence on KL divergence.

The paper attempts to connect BSTs, B-trees, prediction robustness, and locality-aware dynamic access in one framework, and the synthetic experiments are directionally consistent with the static theory.
weaknesses: The novelty relative to classical biased search trees, weighted randomized treaps, weighted skip lists, and near-optimal static BST constructions is not adequately established. The main static guarantee may be obtainable from known weighted randomized search structures, so the paper needs a much sharper prior-work comparison.

The dynamic working-set claim is not convincing as stated. The definition uses a future next-access quantity; for the currently accessed key it appears to rely on future information or on an unclear time indexing of when priorities are updated. This is not the standard online working-set property, and the paper does not cleanly separate clairvoyant, predicted, and online guarantees.

Several proof steps are under-justified. In particular, the cost of changing a weight/priority is asserted rather than proved, the B-treap extension imports high-probability guarantees with little detail, and the composition of tier-wise B-treaps into a valid B-tree needs a more careful invariant and update-cost argument.

The experiments are too limited for the breadth of the claims. They use only synthetic distributions, report comparison counts rather than wall-clock/cache behavior, include no real learned predictor or real workload, and provide no dynamic working-set or external-memory B-tree experiments.

Presentation and reproducibility are weak in places: figure-axis descriptions are inconsistent, some theorem statements mix log bases or BST/B-tree notation, high-probability notation is confusing, and implementation details/code availability are not sufficient to reproduce the empirical results confidently.

strengths: The static composite-priority construction is simple and appealing: grouping keys by coarse weight tiers and randomizing within tiers gives an intuitive route to expected depth O(log(1/w_x)).
The paper addresses a relevant limitation of prior learning-augmented BST work by targeting arbitrary access-frequency distributions rather than only Zipfian ones.
The robustness discussion for static predictions is clean at a high level: using predicted frequencies naturally yields a cross-entropy/KL-divergence overhead.
The B-Tree and dynamic extensions are well-motivated and, if made rigorous, would broaden the contribution beyond a static BST variant.
weaknesses: The novelty is not convincingly established relative to classical biased/static-optimal search trees and randomized weighted search structures. Static optimality from known or predicted frequencies is a long-studied goal, and the paper needs a much sharper account of what is technically new beyond a simple Treap implementation of known biased-search ideas.

Several dynamic and update claims appear under-justified. In particular, the claimed weight-update cost O(|log(w'/w)|) does not follow from the stated delete/insert or depth bounds, and discontinuities from the floor-based tiering can plausibly cause nonlocal restructuring even for small weight changes near tier boundaries. This affects the credibility of the dynamic working-set and robustness results, which rely on update costs.

The working-set guarantee is not the standard online working-set property: for the accessed item, the defined score depends on the next future access. The paper acknowledges this only briefly and effectively assumes a strong future-predicting oracle, but the claims and terminology make the result sound more online and operational than it is.

The B-Treap reduction is sketched rather than fully justified. It invokes a result for uniformly random priorities inside a more structured tiered-priority construction, and the combined-tree maintenance, node-capacity, and high-probability guarantees are not explained with enough precision for a theory-heavy contribution.

The empirical evaluation is weak compared with the claims. It is almost entirely synthetic, gives limited implementation detail and statistical reporting, does not evaluate the dynamic/working-set or B-Tree claims, and uses baselines that do not include strong static-optimal constructions or realistic learned-index systems.

Some experimental claims are suspicious or at least insufficiently explained. Under a uniform distribution, the proposed learned Treap should essentially reduce to a random Treap because all weights have the same tier, yet the text claims it outperforms randomized Treaps and balanced trees. This raises concerns about implementation or measurement fairness.

Presentation quality is uneven, with notation errors and inconsistent statements, such as log bases changing, malformed theorem statements, confusing use of delta in probability claims, and proof/caption inconsistencies around interval versus working-set size. These issues make reproduction and verification harder.

strengths: The paper presents a simple and appealing composite-priority construction for Treaps. The main static argument, grouping keys by tiers of log log(1/w), is clean and gives an intuitive route to expected depth O(log(1/w_x)) for arbitrary access distributions, improving over prior learning-augmented Treap analyses restricted to Zipfian assumptions.

The static robustness result is natural and well motivated: using predicted frequencies q yields a cross-entropy bound and an additive KL-divergence interpretation relative to the entropy-optimal cost.

The paper connects the construction to B-Treaps and external-memory search, and the broader objective of unifying learned frequency information with classical randomized search trees is relevant and potentially useful.

The experimental results, while limited, are consistent with the static theory and include comparisons to both classical balanced trees and prior learning-augmented baselines under several synthetic distributions.
weaknesses: The dynamic working-set result is not convincing as written. The analysis appears to charge the access at time i using the priority/score for the currently accessed key after that key's score has changed, but updating that priority normally requires first finding the node. Without a precise model allowing free direct pointers or pre-access updates, the access/update ordering seems to undercount the true cost.

The working-set definition is future-looking: at access time i it uses the interval until the next access of the same item. This can be useful as a prediction target, but it is not the standard online working-set quantity unless the indexing and update timing are shifted carefully. The theorem statements do not clearly separate oracle knowledge, prediction, and realizable online operations.

Several proof details for the B-Treap and update guarantees are too terse. In particular, the claimed weight-update cost O(|log(w'/w)|) is asserted from delete/insert-like reasoning that would more directly give costs depending on both old and new depths, and the adaptation of Golovin's uniform-priority B-Treap guarantee to tiered shifted priorities needs a more explicit argument.

The empirical evaluation is narrow: it is entirely synthetic, does not evaluate the dynamic working-set data structure, does not test the external-memory/B-Tree claims in a realistic block-I/O setting, and gives limited implementation detail. This leaves the more ambitious claims essentially unvalidated empirically.

The contribution's novelty should be positioned more carefully against classical static optimal BST constructions and entropy-based search trees. The paper shows a neat Treap-based construction, but static optimality from frequencies is classical, so the added value is mainly simplicity, update compatibility, and prediction robustness rather than a fundamentally new optimality guarantee.

Presentation issues reduce confidence: there are mismatches between theorem statements and proofs, occasional base/log inconsistencies, imprecise high-probability claims, undefined edge cases for first/last accesses in the dynamic definitions, and figure/axis text inconsistencies. These are not all fatal, but together they make reproduction and verification harder.

strengths: The static composite-priority construction is simple and appealing: grouping keys by roughly log log(1/w) tiers and randomizing within tiers gives a clean route to expected O(log(1/w)) depth and hence entropy-style/static-optimal access cost when accurate frequencies are known.
The paper attempts to give a unified treatment for BSTs and external-memory B-Trees, and the high-level connection to B-Treaps is natural and potentially useful.

The robustness observation for static frequency misspecification is conceptually clear: using predicted probabilities q leads to a cross-entropy-type bound, so KL divergence is the right error measure up to constants.
weaknesses: The main contribution may be less original than claimed. The paper does not adequately position the static result against classical biased/weighted randomized search trees, biased skip lists, nearly optimal BSTs, and related entropy-optimal dictionary constructions. Without this comparison, it is hard to judge whether the composite priority rule is a substantive advance or a rediscovery/repackaging.

Several dynamic claims are not convincingly supported. The working-set priority requires next-access information, so the result is essentially oracle/offline unless a realistic prediction model is specified. The paper advertises online self-reorganization, but the theorem relies on knowing or predicting future access intervals and does not evaluate such predictions.

The update-cost analysis appears underjustified and possibly incorrect. The paper repeatedly claims that changing a weight from w to w' costs O(|log(w'/w)|) rotations/touched nodes, but this does not follow from the stated Treap insertion/deletion lemma; deletion plus insertion would give a bound depending on the absolute depths, not only the ratio. This claim is central to the dynamic cost bounds.

The B-Treap extension is sketched at too high a level. The proof relies on decomposing by tiers and combining B-Treaps, but it does not fully justify that the resulting structure satisfies the required B-Tree invariants, occupancy/branching constraints, or Golovin-style guarantees under nonuniform tiered priorities.

The empirical evaluation is weak relative to the claims. It is entirely synthetic, uses perfect or highly controlled frequency predictions, does not evaluate the dynamic/working-set method, does not include real learned predictors or real workloads, and omits important baselines such as static optimal/near-optimal weighted trees or classical weighted randomized trees.

Some empirical conclusions are unsurprising or potentially unfair: methods using exact frequencies are compared to generic balanced trees under frequency-skewed workloads, while prediction cost, construction cost, update cost, and memory/cache behavior are largely excluded.

The presentation has many notation inconsistencies and proof-level slips, including base mismatches in Theorem 4.4, repeated or mislabeled theorem titles, self-referential/incorrect corollary references, typos in dynamic proofs, and imprecise statements such as claiming the KL overhead is exact despite only proving asymptotic bounds. These issues make reproduction and verification difficult.

The defined quantity uses the next access after the current time, so it is future-looking rather than the standard online working-set bound based on recency. strengths: The composite-priority construction for Treaps is simple and intuitive, and the main static BST depth argument is largely convincing: grouping keys by log-log weight tiers and randomizing within each tier gives expected depth O(log(1/w_x)).
The paper targets a meaningful limitation of prior learning-augmented BST work by aiming to remove the Zipfian-distribution assumption and obtain static optimality for arbitrary access distributions.
The robustness analysis for static frequency prediction is natural: using predicted probabilities leads to a cross-entropy-style bound and connects excess cost to KL divergence.
The manuscript attempts a broad treatment, including B-Trees/external memory, dynamic working-set behavior, and empirical comparisons against several classic and learned data structures.
weaknesses: The dynamic results are not sufficiently convincing. The locally dynamic proof appears to assume that the priority of the requested item can be updated before paying the search cost, or otherwise uses the new score to bound the current access depth. In a normal search tree operation the item must first be located under the old tree, so the stated working-set access bound is not justified as written.

The proof of the general locally dynamic theorem seems false for arbitrary locally changed scores: the update-cost term |log(w_{i-1,x(i)}/w_{i,x(i)})| is bounded by current-access score terms, but the old score of the currently accessed item need not have appeared in the previous access-cost sum. This undermines the dynamic and robustness claims built on that theorem.

The relation to classical biased/weighted search trees and weighted randomized Treaps is underdeveloped. The static guarantee resembles known weighted search-tree results, so the originality and precise improvement over prior non-learning-augmented data-structure literature are unclear.

The B-Tree extension is sketched rather than fully established. It relies heavily on Golovin's B-Treap result under assumptions that are not carefully checked for tier-restricted subtrees, and the high-probability statements use confusing notation such as reusing delta both as an exponent parameter and a failure probability.

The empirical evaluation is narrow and raises reproducibility/interpretation concerns. It uses only synthetic point-query access costs, no real workloads, no dynamic-working-set experiments, no external-memory/B-Treap evaluation, no update costs, and limited details about implementations and prediction generation.

Some experimental claims appear inconsistent or at least poorly explained. For example, under a truly uniform frequency distribution the proposed Treap should behave like a random Treap, yet the plots show a large advantage; the text also misdescribes the x-axis as number of unique items while the figures show number of accesses.

Presentation quality is uneven, with notation/base inconsistencies, missing parentheses, repeated text, typos, and minor proof errors such as a corollary referring to itself. These issues make informed verification harder than it should be.

strengths: The core static construction is simple and appealing: the composite priority based on floor(log log(1/w)) plus random tie-breaking gives an intuitive route to expected depth O(log(1/w)) for arbitrary predicted weights.

The paper connects the construction to static optimality and prediction robustness in a clean way; the cross-entropy/KL interpretation is natural and helps clarify how inaccurate frequency predictions affect expected access cost.
The manuscript addresses a relevant gap relative to prior learning-augmented BST work that assumed Zipfian access distributions, and it also attempts to cover external-memory B-tree variants.
The exposition of the main static Treap argument is mostly understandable, with useful counterexamples showing why simpler priority choices can fail.
weaknesses: The dynamic/working-set claims are not convincing as stated. The algorithm appears to update the priority of the queried key before paying the search cost, which requires already having a pointer to the item; without such an assumption this is a causality issue, and with such an assumption the dictionary-search model changes substantially.

The claimed update cost O(|log(w'/w)|) is under-justified and seems false for priority changes that require rotations through a large tier. A delete-and-reinsert argument would give costs depending on old and new depths, not merely the logarithmic ratio, and the dynamic theorems rely heavily on this step.

The “working-set” quantity is future-looking, based on the next access rather than the standard past working-set number. This may be meaningful with a strong oracle, but the paper overstates it as the usual working-set property and does not clearly separate online, offline, and prediction-oracle assumptions.

The B-tree extension is promising but too terse: it relies on applying B-Treap guarantees inside tier subtrees and then composing them, but important invariants, update procedures, degree/occupancy guarantees, and high-probability conditions are not fully spelled out.

The empirical evaluation is weak for the scale of the claims. It is entirely synthetic, uses no learned predictor, provides no dynamic/working-set experiments, and omits strong classical baselines such as explicit near-optimal static trees built from frequencies. Some axis descriptions and access-cost magnitudes are confusing, making the experiments hard to interpret.

Several presentation and rigor issues remain: inconsistent bases in theorem statements, probability written as 1-delta while delta is also a branching-factor exponent, a circular typo in the chi-squared robustness proof, and claims such as “exactly m times KL overhead” despite only asymptotic bounds.

This may be fixable by an index shift, but the online timing and initialization need to be stated and proved precisely.

strengths: The core static construction is elegant and easy to state: grouping keys by doubly-logarithmic weight tiers and breaking ties randomly gives a plausible and mostly clear route to expected depth O(log(1/w_x)).
The connection between inaccurate frequency predictions and cross-entropy/KL overhead is natural and useful, and the paper explains it in a way that makes the robustness intuition transparent.
The paper addresses a relevant learning-augmented data-structures problem and attempts to unify BST, B-Tree, static, dynamic, and robustness perspectives in one framework.
weaknesses: The dynamic working-set claim is not convincingly established. The working-set score is defined using the next future access, and the claimed access bound appears to require updating or knowing the accessed item's priority before paying the search cost. This is not the standard online working-set property and needs a much clearer model or a substantially different proof.

The priority-update cost bounds are underjustified and appear problematic. The paper claims updates cost O(|log(w'/w)|), but changing tiers can plausibly require rotations through many nodes in a tier, and the dynamic proofs even resample random offsets, which could cause nontrivial restructuring when the weight itself has not changed.

The static-optimality statements omit the usual additive constant per access. Claims such as O(m Ent(p)) fail or become ill-defined for very low-entropy distributions, e.g. one dominant key; the correct form should be closer to O(m(1+H(p))).

The B-Treap extension is too sketchy for the strength of the claims. Applying Golovin's result separately to tier components and recombining them needs more detail about invariants, node occupancy, update operations, and the stated high-probability guarantees.

The empirical section is not strong enough to support the broad performance claims. It uses only synthetic workloads, has inconsistencies about whether n or m is varied, reports implausibly low comparison counts for some uniform-search settings, and does not evaluate the dynamic or B-Tree claims.
Overall, the static Treap idea is a real merit, but several headline claims, especially dynamic working-set behavior and update robustness, are insufficiently supported at present.

The robustness argument for static frequency prediction is natural and useful: inaccurate weights lead to a cross-entropy bound and an additive KL-divergence interpretation.

This needs a precise cost-ordering model and proof that the claimed working-set bound applies to actual accesses.

The update-cost claims are underjustified. The paper repeatedly uses weight-change costs of O(|log(w'/w)|), but the provided delete-then-insert argument would normally give a sum of depth terms rather than a difference. Since the dynamic and B-Treap bounds rely on these update costs, this is a substantive proof gap.

strengths: The central static idea is simple and appealing: quantizing weights into logarithmic tiers and using random offsets gives an easy expected-depth bound of O(log(1/w_x)), which yields static optimality from frequency predictions for arbitrary distributions.

The paper identifies a real limitation of the Lin et al. frequency-priority treap under non-Zipfian distributions and gives a plausible construction that avoids the obvious monotone-priority failure mode.
The robustness framing through cross entropy/KL divergence is natural for the static setting and helps connect prediction quality to access cost.

Extending the construction toward B-treaps and external-memory search is a potentially useful direction, and the manuscript includes proofs and related-work discussion rather than only empirical claims.
weaknesses: The dynamic/working-set contribution is not convincing as written. The definition of work(i,x) uses future accesses, and the algorithmic timing is unclear: the proofs appear to update the accessed item's priority before the search, which would require already locating the item or having a pointer. If the update is after access, the stated depth bound uses the wrong score index. This undermines a major claimed contribution.

The claimed update bounds for changing weights are not adequately justified and may be false under the discontinuous tiered priority rule. A tiny change in weight can cross a tier boundary and require many rotations, while the paper states an O(|log(w'/w)|) expected bound by appealing only to insertion/deletion depth.

The empirical section has serious credibility issues. Under a uniform distribution, the proposed treap should reduce essentially to a randomized treap, but the plots show a large performance gap over the randomized-treap baseline. This suggests an implementation, measurement, or baseline mismatch that is not explained.

The experiments are narrow and underdescribed: only small synthetic distributions are used, dynamic/working-set behavior is not experimentally evaluated, real traces are absent, update costs/cache behavior are ignored, and the figures/text contain inconsistencies about whether the x-axis is number of accesses or unique items.

The novelty is not fully established relative to classical biased/weighted randomized search trees and other static optimal BST constructions. Since static optimal search trees from frequencies are long known, the paper needs a sharper account of what the treap construction adds beyond existing weighted randomized or biased search-tree methods.

Several theoretical claims are overstated relative to the proofs. For example, the KL robustness is presented as an exact additive overhead, but the theorem only gives big-O upper bounds; high-probability statements in the B-tree section are imprecise; and some appendix proofs rely on informal reductions to prior B-treap results without enough detail.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a theory-heavy ICML submission: notation is inconsistent between BSTs and B-trees, some theorem statements contain apparent typos or mismatched logarithm bases, and important operational assumptions for prediction oracles and pointer availability are not specified.

strengths: The core static construction is simple and appealing: bucket priorities by approximately log log(1/w) and use random offsets within buckets. The proof idea for expected depth O(log(1/w)) is clear and plausibly correct for BSTs.
The paper gives a useful conceptual bridge between learning-augmented Treaps and arbitrary access distributions, removing the Zipfian restriction of Lin et al. for the static setting.

The robustness observation for static frequency prediction is natural and informative: using predicted probabilities yields a cross-entropy-style cost, so KL divergence gives the right additive degradation up to constants.
The manuscript attempts to connect BSTs, B-Trees, prediction robustness, and working-set behavior in one framework, which is a potentially valuable direction.
weaknesses: The dynamic/working-set claims are not convincingly supported. The analysis appears to let the data structure update the accessed key's priority before paying the search cost, but in a search tree one must first find the item unless a pointer is already available. If the update happens after the access, the stated depth bound for that access does not follow. This is a central correctness issue.

The claimed update cost O(|log_B(w'/w)|) is not adequately proved and seems incompatible with the stated delete-and-reinsert justification, which would normally give costs depending on log(1/w)+log(1/w'). Re-sampling random offsets can also change ordering within a tier even when the weight ratio is small. This undermines the dynamic total-cost bounds.

The working-set score uses next(i,x), i.e. future accesses. The paper frames this as learning-augmented or online self-reorganization, but the theorem essentially assumes a strong future oracle and provides no convincing causal prediction model or empirical evaluation of such predictions.

The B-Tree extension is too sketchy for the weight it carries. The proof relies on applying Golovin's B-Treap result inside tiers with insufficient justification, inconsistent parameter conditions, and unclear high-probability statements. It is not clear that the external-memory claims follow as stated.

Novelty is overstated. Static optimal BSTs from frequencies are classical, and the paper does not adequately position the construction against weighted/biased randomized search trees, biased search trees, optimal alphabetic trees, or other known entropy-optimal dictionary structures.

The empirical evaluation is weak. It uses only synthetic distributions, small-scale settings, comparison counts rather than wall-clock/cache behavior, no real workloads, no dynamic or B-Tree experiments despite major claims, and no comparison to static optimal or near-optimal frequency-based trees.

Presentation and reproducibility are below the expected standard. Several statements contain notation errors, base-log inconsistencies, duplicated theorem titles, undefined or inconsistent variables, and proof steps that are asserted rather than derived. Experimental implementation details are also insufficient for reproduction.
